candidates.attacker_control: A remote user can control the submitted SAMLResponse XML, including the response Issuer, Destination, InResponseTo, Status, and an Assertion with an arbitrary principal/NameID, even though the user does not possess the IdP signing key. For an SP-initiated flow, the user can initiate the login normally to obtain the broker auth-session RelayState and can decode the generated AuthnRequest ID for InResponseTo. If wantAssertionsSigned is also enabled, the assertion-signature validity check is still gated by validateSignature, so the attacker can satisfy the presence check without producing a trustworthy signature.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: I checked all assignments to setValidateSignature: no later default overrides the metadata-derived value. The result is read directly by SAMLEndpoint. If the imported metadata has WantAuthnRequestsSigned=true, validation remains enabled, and an administrator can manually enable Validate Signature after import. If the realm uses only OIDC, this path is not applicable. The test is deployment/configuration-dependent and was not executed.
candidates.impact: Authentication bypass in the SAML broker: a remote attacker may be able to submit a forged response and be logged in as a chosen brokered principal, leading to account takeover or unauthorized access to clients/sessions associated with that identity in affected deployments.
candidates.prerequisites: The realm must have a SAML identity provider imported from metadata whose WantAuthnRequestsSigned attribute is absent or false, and an administrator must not have manually re-enabled Validate Signature afterward. The realm and broker endpoint must be reachable, and the target client/flow must use that IdP.
candidates.root_cause: SAMLIdentityProviderFactory.parseConfig initializes validateSignature from idpDescriptor.isWantAuthnRequestsSigned(). WantAuthnRequestsSigned describes whether the IdP wants AuthnRequests signed by the SP; it does not describe whether the IdP signs SAML responses or assertions. An omitted or false value therefore produces an imported SAML IdP with validateSignature=false. SAMLEndpoint only verifies the response signature and the assertion signature validity when that flag is true, so the imported configuration disables cryptographic verification of attacker-supplied SAML responses.
candidates.title: SAML IdP metadata import disables response signature validation from an unrelated flag
candidates.trace: 1) SAMLIdentityProviderFactory.parseConfig sets both setWantAuthnRequestsSigned and setValidateSignature from idpDescriptor.isWantAuthnRequestsSigned() (lines 129-131), so absent/false metadata yields validateSignature=false. 2) On an incoming SAMLResponse, SAMLEndpoint.handleSamlResponse checks destination but wraps the response signature verification in if (config.isValidateSignature()) (lines 646-655). 3) In handleLoginResponse, signatureNotValid is evaluated as signed && config.isValidateSignature() && !AssertionUtil.isSignatureValid(...), so an untrusted assertion signature is not checked when validateSignature is false (lines 470-480). 4) The broker then derives the principal and subject from the attacker-controlled assertion and calls callback.authenticated(identity), potentially resolving to an existing federated user/session. The same conditional design also means a configured wantAssertionsSigned flag is not a substitute for enabling validateSignature.
candidates.unverified: The attack was not runtime-confirmed. I did not construct or validate a forged SAML XML payload against the running broker, and I did not verify schema validation and first-broker-login behavior end to end. Confidence is based on the explicit source control flow; prevalence depends on how the realm's SAML IdP metadata was imported and subsequently configured.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

coverage_summary: The scope reports 5,890 model-visible source files, with no files excluded for path sensitivity, symlinks, or size over 5 MiB; binary-like files are skipped when a NUL byte is found. I inspected SAML core parsing/signature code, the SAML broker endpoint and metadata importer, OIDC token/signature paths, admin authorization checks and client/export endpoints, theme resource handling, credential providers, and selected client-policy/authorization code. This was a targeted review of security-sensitive paths, not an exhaustive line-by-line audit of all 5,890 files.
limitations: No code was executed, no tests or scanners were run, and no running Keycloak instance was used.
The repository is large; many modules and generated/static resources were not inspected in depth.
The SAML finding depends on deployment configuration and on behavior of the XML schema parser and broker login flow that was not dynamically validated.
No patch history, CVE metadata, external advisory data, or ground-truth labels were available; conclusions are based only on the assigned source snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: View-only administrators can retrieve client secrets
rejected_leads.reason: ClientResource.getClientSecret() and client installation endpoints use requireView, and ModelToRepresentation includes client secrets. This is potentially a real disclosure, but Keycloak's view-client semantics may intentionally include credential reads; I did not select it because the policy intent and impact are less clear than the SAML signature bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: Mixed encrypted and plaintext assertion signature bypass
rejected_leads.reason: XMLSignatureUtil.validate only counts plaintext Assertion elements when checking for unsigned assertions mixed with signed ones, and SAMLEndpoint decrypts only the first assertion choice. A signed plaintext assertion could potentially serve as a signature anchor while a malicious encrypted assertion is used as the identity, but this requires additional IdP-initiated-flow and configuration conditions and was not selected over the direct metadata-import flaw.

rejected_leads.lead: Admin authorization-dialog stored XSS via unescaped resource names
rejected_leads.reason: AuthzDialog builds a delete confirmation message by concatenating names into HTML and passes it to $sce.trustAsHtml. This is a plausible stored XSS, but exploitation depends on another administrator opening the delete dialog for an attacker-influenced name, with lower direct impact than the unauthenticated SAML authentication bypass.

summary: Reviewed the Keycloak source snapshot for high-impact, source-supported vulnerabilities. The strongest lead is in SAML IdP metadata import: an unrelated IdP preference about signing AuthnRequests is used to decide whether Keycloak validates SAML responses/assertions. When metadata omits or disables WantAuthnRequestsSigned, the imported IdP configuration has validateSignature=false, and the broker accepts forged SAML responses without cryptographic verification. I also examined a potential view-only client-secret exposure and a mixed encrypted/plaintext assertion validation gap, but did not select them as candidates.
